Floating-Toolbar.tagline: A 52-pixel launcher bar that floats above everything: groups that drop down, icons that stay put, and files you can drag straight onto it.
summary: Most launchers want a dock, a start menu or an installer. This one is a strip 52 pixels tall that stays on top of other windows and does nothing until you click: groups that open a list, entries pinned to the bar that launch in one click, and a right-click menu for adding, editing and removing both.

It is a .NET 8 WinForms app with no third-party packages — the bar, its buttons, the dark renderer, the icon loader and the fullscreen detector are all in the repository. Dropping a file, shortcut, folder or URL on the bar adds it as an entry and takes the target's own shell icon; an entry whose target has disappeared reports the failure instead of taking the app down.

Two things make it survive a working day: Ctrl+Alt+Space shows or hides the bar from any application, and an optional auto-hide pulls it out of the way while a fullscreen app has focus, then puts it back when focus returns. Settings are a single JSON file under %APPDATA%, so a whole layout can be copied between machines.

highlights.title: Groups that drop down
highlights.text: Office, browsers and Windows tools each take one slot on the bar; clicking opens the list, and a group can append the user's own browser favourites as a sub-menu.

highlights.title: Drag to arrange, in both directions
highlights.text: Entries reorder inside an open drop-down and groups reorder along the bar, with a blue insertion line showing where the item will land before you let go.

highlights.title: Drop files from Explorer
highlights.text: Files, shortcuts, folders and URLs dropped on the bar become working buttons carrying the target's own icon; a target that no longer exists shows a message instead of crashing the launch.

highlights.title: Out of the way when it should be
highlights.text: Ctrl+Alt+Space toggles the bar globally, and auto-hide restores it the moment the fullscreen app loses focus.

highlights.title: Small on purpose
highlights.text: One executable, no NuGet packages and no background service: the self-contained single file is the same project published with one extra flag.

quickstart.label: Download and run
quickstart.note: Unzip Floating-Toolbar-win-x64.zip anywhere and run FloatingToolbar.exe — the published build is self-contained, so nothing else needs installing.

quickstart.label: Add your own buttons
quickstart.code: Right-click the bar for New group / Add application / Pin an application
quickstart.note: Dragging files from Explorer onto the bar works too. Right-click a group for Add application, Edit group, Rename group and Remove group.

quickstart.label: Build from source
quickstart.note: The project targets net8.0-windows; the shipped single file is the same project published with -r win-x64 --self-contained.

requirements: .NET 8 desktop runtime, or the self-contained zip

RibbonWinForms.tagline: An Office-style ribbon for Windows Forms that still works inside the designer.
summary: The ribbon draws a tabbed command bar — tabs, panels, buttons — on top of an ordinary Windows Forms window. The point of this fork is that it behaves the same at runtime and inside Visual Studio's out-of-process designer, which is where ribbon controls usually fall apart.

It is published as a package rather than a loose DLL: the package is what puts the control in the toolbox, so a project that adds the package and a project that references a DLL end up in different places. Per-panel spacing and padding knobs control how densely the groups sit.

highlights.title: Designer-safe by design
highlights.text: Ported to .NET 10 and repaired so the control renders in the designer, not just at runtime — including the toolbox entry.

highlights.title: One package, every project
highlights.text: The same dotnet add package call per project, so each one gets the toolbox reference instead of a hand-copied DLL.

highlights.title: Spacing you can tune
highlights.text: Per-panel spacing and padding settings, plus a short guide in the README for keeping groups and buttons aligned.

highlights.title: Built on every push
highlights.text: A GitHub Actions workflow compiles the branch so the .NET 10 port does not silently rot.

changes: Fixed 'cannot create an instance of abstract class RibbonItem' when adding items through the orb menu, recent and option collection editors in the Properties window.
The orb drop-down now autosizes to its content at runtime — width fits the menu, recent and option items, and the empty recent pane collapses.
The design-time orb menu sizes itself to its entries and button captions, so text no longer truncates.
Widened the design-time orb menu to 300px so the add-button captions and longer item text no longer truncate.
Fixed a second design-server crash when creating orb menu items in the designer — layout code tried to get a graphics handle from the drop-down window, which has no handle at design time.
Fixed a crash when clicking the blank orb menu's add buttons in the designer — the code touched the real drop-down window, which does not exist at design time.
The blank menu's add buttons now show text labels (New Menu Item, New Separator, New Recent Item, New Option Item) in a two-by-two grid.
Added Office/Microsoft ribbon keywords to the package tags and repository topics: microsoft-ribbon, ribbon-ui, winribbon.
Package metadata now credits WindowsRibbon (github.com/harborsiem/WindowsRibbon) and RibbonWinForms in the description, authors and copyright.
Release notes cover the design-time orb menu work.

An empty orb menu now shows the same blank frame and design-time add buttons (menu item, separator, recent, option) that the real drop-down paints in design mode; clicking them creates the matching entry.
Removed the "+ Menu / + Recent / + Options" text rows from the design-time orb menu — they were designer affordances that do not exist in the real drop-down.
Fixed the orb menu paint offset in the designer: glyph paint graphics are already in adorner coordinates, so the menu is now translated by +the ribbon's adorner offset.

The design-time orb menu is now painted through the adorner glyph instead of OnPaintAdornments, so it is no longer clipped at the ribbon's bottom edge and can hang below the ribbon like the real drop-down.

Clicking the orb in the designer opens the orb menu on the design surface: menu, recent and option items with their icons, row highlighting, click-to-select, and add-entry glyphs — the same approach the panel "Add Control" menu already used. Runtime behaviour is unchanged.
Clicking a ribbon tab in the designer now switches the tab and shows that tab's page, matched against the bounds the design surface draws.
Added SelectedIndex and SelectedIndexChanged to the Ribbon, so the visible tab can be chosen from the Properties window and is saved with the form.
Added discoverability tags (ribbon-framework, ribbon-tools, windows-ribbon, win-ribbon) alongside the existing package tags.
Package description aligned with the project tagline; same .NET 10 port as 1.0.0-net10.

First release: the .NET 10 port, with a working out-of-process designer, selectable tabs/panels/items, Add Tab / Add Panel / Add Control pills, collection editors in the Properties grid, and no design-time assembly loaded at runtime.

quickstart.note: Add it to each project that needs the ribbon, then the control appears in the toolbox.

quickstart.label: Work on the source
quickstart.note: The port lives on the net10 branch, which is the repository default.

GraphicsWorkshop.tagline: A desktop graphics workstation: edit an image, place objects on a design surface, rotate them in place.
summary: Graphics Workshop started years ago in VB.NET as a collection of half-finished experiments. It was rebuilt in C# on top of the .NET 10 ribbon fork, which is why both languages are still visible in the tree.

The app has two halves: a canvas for drawing and editing graphics, and a design surface where objects are added, positioned and rotated. It is explicitly unfinished — the README says so plainly and asks for contributors rather than pretending the thing is done.

highlights.title: Design surface, not just a canvas
highlights.text: Objects are added to a surface, moved to a position and rotated — the object model lives in a separate control repository.

highlights.title: Powered by the ribbon fork
highlights.text: The whole shell was rebuilt around the .NET 10 ribbon, so the command bar is the same control that ships as Dwain.RibbonLib.

highlights.title: A long road, kept public
highlights.text: VB.NET roots, then C#; the repository is open in its unfinished state so the work can continue with help.

highlights.title: Honest about status
highlights.text: Described by its author as incomplete — not a demo dressed up as a release.

quickstart.label: Clone and open the solution
quickstart.note: Open GraphicsWorkshop.sln in Visual Studio and let it restore the packages.config references, then run frmGraphicDesigner.

requirements: Visual Studio 2022 with the Windows Forms workload

DesignSurfaceCSharp.tagline: The object model and surface control that Graphics Workshop is built on.
summary: Two projects do the real work here: GraphicObjects holds the shapes and their properties, and GraphicsSurface is the control that paints them, hit-tests them and hosts the rotation handles.

It ships as source rather than a package. There is no README, so the three sample apps — WindowsFormsApp1, WindowsFormsApp2 and WindowsFormsApp3 — are the documentation: each one drops the surface on a form so you can see what it does.

highlights.title: Reusable object model
highlights.text: GraphicObjects describes the shapes independently of any window, so the model can be reused by another host.

highlights.title: A surface control
highlights.text: GraphicsSurface owns painting, selection and manipulation, with its own rotation cursor art in the resources folder.

highlights.title: Three runnable samples
highlights.text: The sample apps are the quickest way in: open one, run it, watch the surface behave.

highlights.title: Source-only, deliberately
highlights.text: No package and no README — copy the projects you need rather than taking a dependency.

quickstart.label: Clone the source
quickstart.note: Open one of the sample projects directly in Visual Studio — there is no solution file.

requirements: Visual Studio with the Windows Forms workload

MOTW-Cleaner.tagline: Strips Mark of the Web from downloaded files so Windows stops blocking them.
summary: Files that arrive from the internet carry a Zone.Identifier stream — Mark of the Web. Windows uses it to open documents in Protected View and to refuse to run what it does not trust, which is why a perfectly fine download sits there refusing to open.

MOTW Cleaner removes that marker from the files and folders you choose, in a small WinForms window, and reports progress while it works. It is distributed as an MSI installer, with its own changelog page hosted on GitHub Pages.

highlights.title: Unblock in one pass
highlights.text: Point it at files or folders and it clears the zone identifier instead of making you open file properties one by one.

highlights.title: Made for downloaded archives
highlights.text: Drop a zip, extract, clean — the workflow the tool was built around.

highlights.title: Installer, not a zip of DLLs
highlights.text: Ships as MOTW.Installer.msi from the 1.3.0 release, so it installs and uninstalls like normal software.

highlights.title: Its own changelog
highlights.text: A separate HTML page under dwainsnickles.github.io/MOTW-Cleaner documents what changed in each version.

quickstart.label: Download the installer
quickstart.note: Run the MSI, then open MOTW Cleaner and pick the files or folder to unblock.

quickstart.note: Open MOTW Cleaner.slnx in Visual Studio, restore packages.config, and run.

Maui-basic-VLC-Player-Tutorial.tagline: How to get VLC playing MP4 and HLS streams inside a .NET MAUI app, written down so nobody else loses the weeks.
summary: This repository is a write-up, not a codebase: the README is the whole thing. It walks through wiring LibVLCSharp into .NET MAUI — the packages, the handler registration in MauiProgram.cs, the MediaPlayer setup, and the Grid layout with a control bar over a VideoView.
The author's note is refreshingly direct: MAUI video support was still rough, it took weeks to reach a working player, and this is part one of what is meant to become a series.

highlights.title: The packages that actually matter
highlights.text: LibVLCSharp, LibVLCSharp.MAUI, plus the native VideoLAN.LibVLC builds for Android, Windows and iOS.

highlights.title: Handler registration
highlights.text: The piece most tutorials skip: mapping VideoView to VideoViewHandler in MauiProgram.cs and calling Core.Initialize().

highlights.title: A usable layout
highlights.text: A two-row Grid — volume, mute, fullscreen and title-bar toggles above a VideoView that fills the rest.

highlights.title: HLS, not just MP4
highlights.text: The sample plays an HLS test stream, which is where naive player samples usually stop working.

quickstart.note: Then follow the README: register the VideoView handler, call Core.Initialize(), create the LibVLC and MediaPlayer instances.

AutoUpdater.NET.XML-Creator-master.tagline: A form that writes the manifest XML AutoUpdater.NET needs, so you never hand-edit an update file again.
summary: AutoUpdater.NET decides whether to update an app by reading an XML manifest: version, download URL, checksum, changelog. Getting that file right by hand is where self-updating desktop apps break.

This app builds the manifest in a guided form, then writes the file. The March 2023 pass added a version picker that reads the new executable, an algorithm generator for every supported hash type, radio buttons for the update types, support for the <args> tag, and required-field enforcement on the first two steps.

highlights.title: Version read from the build
highlights.text: A button picks the new exe and fills in its version, instead of you copying it out of the assembly info.

highlights.title: Checksums generated, not guessed
highlights.text: One button creates the algorithm value for all supported types.

highlights.title: Guided, and it enforces it
highlights.text: The first two steps cannot be skipped — they are the minimum a manifest needs to work.

highlights.title: Every tag, including optional ones
highlights.text: Update types, <args>, changelog URL and the optional tags are all exposed in the form.

quickstart.label: Clone and build
quickstart.note: Open AutoUpdater.NET.sln, build AutoUpdaterTest, and run it. AutoUpdaterXML.xml in the root shows the shape of the output.

requirements: Visual Studio with the Windows Forms workload

pc-medic.tagline: A portable maintenance console: startup control, registry and shortcut audits, winget upgrades, driver search and benchmark rig setup in one window.
summary: PC Medic is one executable with no installer, no background service and no telemetry. Each page is a job people actually run on a struggling machine: what starts with Windows, why the boot is slow, what is filling the disk, which applications are out of date, and which registry keys or shortcuts point at files that no longer exist.

The rule behind every destructive action is that it must be reversible or provable. Cleaned files go to the Recycle Bin, registry edits write a .reg backup first, boot tweaks store the previous values in JSON, and the audits list only entries whose target is genuinely missing rather than whatever looks suspicious.

That proof is a missing file or folder on a mounted fixed drive, never a guess. A finding arrives with its switch already on, because the missing path was checked before the row was drawn; review-only rows stay off and untickable, and their tooltip says why the target could not be resolved. Programs uninstall from a bin on their own row, and anything that takes time reports on itself rather than freezing the window.

highlights.title: Audits that prove what they claim
highlights.text: The registry audit reports keys whose target file or folder is gone and nothing else, and ticks each proven entry for removal; the shortcut audit resolves every .lnk through IShellLinkW and flags only the ones that no longer point anywhere, keeping a proven dead target apart from a link it could not resolve at all.

highlights.title: Updates with what Windows ships
highlights.text: winget streams each application upgrade into a progress bar on that row, and a bin on the row starts the app's own uninstaller, so removal is never a detour through another page. The Windows Update agent supplies the driver search, and nothing is fetched from a third-party server.

highlights.title: Long jobs say what they are doing
highlights.text: Every scan covers its results with a centred LOADING ##% plate: real counts where the work reports progress, an estimate that never finishes early where the call is opaque. Any wait that reports nothing at all raises a WORKING strip across the bottom of the shell.

highlights.title: Benchmark rigs that install themselves
highlights.text: The benchmark grid shows which portable rigs are present and installs the missing ones through winget, one dialog with a bar per download, then re-detects the suite so nothing stays marked missing.

highlights.title: Portable, and honest about rights
highlights.text: asInvoker, no drivers and no scheduled tasks of its own; elevation is opt-in per action and the UI always states whether you are a standard user.

quickstart.label: Download the portable build
quickstart.note: Unzip it anywhere, a USB stick included, and run PC Medic.exe. The suite zip puts Disk Defrag next to it, and the Maintenance page finds it automatically.

quickstart.label: Build it from source
quickstart.code:
git clone https://github.com/DwainSnickles/pc-medic
cd pc-medic
dotnet build "PC Medic.csproj"
quickstart.note: The portable layout lands in bin/Debug/net10.0-windows/.

requirements: .NET 10 desktop runtime, or the SDK to build it
Administrator rights only for the actions that need them
